attributes.comment:
I am writing as an operator of a clinical research site (Yuma Clinical Trials, in Yuma, Arizona) and as the founder of a contract research organization (DSCS CRO) that supports community-based investigator sites. My perspective is from the site side of clinical research, which I believe is underrepresented in most policy comments on this RFI.

Three points:

1. AI-enabled optimization of early-phase trials must include site-level operational data, not just sponsor-level enrollment and protocol data. The predominant data sources cited for AI optimization are sponsor EDC, EHR networks (Tempus, TriNetX, Veeva, Datavant), and ClinicalTrials.gov. These are necessary but not sufficient. They miss the operational reality at the site: actual screen-fail rates by inclusion criterion, time from referral to first dose, source-document burden by visit, and staff bandwidth constraints. A pilot that draws only from sponsor and EHR data will optimize for sponsor convenience and produce predictions that fail at sites. I would encourage the agency to require pilot participants to demonstrate site-level data inputs, with site consent and benefit-sharing terms documented in the pilot proposal.

2. Diversity Action Plan compliance and AI-enabled site selection should be evaluated together. Hispanic/Latino patients comprise approximately 18 percent of the U.S. population and roughly 8 percent of trial participants. AI site-selection models trained on historical enrollment patterns will systematically under-rank community sites serving underrepresented populations because those sites have shorter histories with industry sponsors, smaller previous-trial counts, and less polished feasibility responses. Without explicit instrumentation, the pilot will accelerate the same coastal-academic-center concentration that DAP guidance is intended to correct. I would encourage the agency to ask pilot proposers to demonstrate how their AI methods address this risk, for example through fairness audits on site-selection recommendations stratified by site catchment demographics.

3. Operational definitions of early-phase optimization should include the cost and time the site bears, not only the sponsor metrics. From a site operator's perspective, AI optimization that compresses sponsor timelines but increases site-side rework (protocol amendments, eDiary churn, frequent inclusion-criterion updates pushed mid-study) is a net negative for the trial ecosystem because it accelerates site burnout in an industry already constrained by CRA and CRC shortages. I would recommend that the pilot evaluation criteria include site-reported burden metrics alongside sponsor-reported speed metrics, and that pilot proposers commit to publishing both.

I support the program's intent and the FDA's leadership on this topic. The 20 to 40 percent trial-time reduction described publicly is plausible if the optimization includes the site as a first-class participant. It is unlikely if it does not.

Respectfully submitted,
Dan Sfera
Founder, DSCS CRO
Operator, Yuma Clinical Trials
